openalex.title: Can Quantum-Mechanical Description of Physical Reality Be Considered Complete?
openalex.abstract: In a complete theory there is an element corresponding to each element of reality. A sufficient condition for the reality of a physical quantity is the possibility of predicting it with certainty, without disturbing the system. In quantum mechanics in the case of two physical quantities described by non-commuting operators, the knowledge of one precludes the knowledge of the other. Then either (1) the description of reality given by the wave function in quantum mechanics is not complete or (2) these two quantities cannot have simultaneous reality. Consideration of the problem of making predictions concerning a system on the basis of measurements made on another system that had previously interacted with it leads to the result that if (1) is false then (2) is also false. One is thus led to conclude that the description of reality as given by a wave function is not complete.

citations.title: The persuasive function of humor in scientific discourse: the case study of “Against ‘Measurement’” by J.S. Bell
contexts: The cat paradox – that Schrödinger introduces as one of the “ ridiculous cases ” 9 to which quantum theory could be applied – illustrates what has become known as the measurement problem of QM (e.g., Dürr and Lazarovici 2020).

Although the arguments of Schrödinger and EPR, challenging the completeness of QM, remain cornerstones of the foundational debate to this day, their immediate e ﬀ ect on the physics community was limited, and the “ tranquilizing philosophy ” of Copenhagen prevailed.

One month later, Schrödinger (1935) joins the discussion with his article featuring the now famous cat thought experiment in which the wavefunction describes the cat ending up in a superposition of dead and alive.
This wavefunction, introduced by Erwin Schrödinger (1926), is not a wave in physical space but a new kind of mathematical object that has no analog in classical (Newtonian) physics.

One of Schrödinger ’ s English translators notes a “ semi-conversational, at times slightly sardonic ﬂ avor ” (Trimmer 1980: 323) which shows not only in the “ ridiculous cases ” but also, for example, in a footnote of the same paper, in which Schrödinger explains that his article was prompted by the EPR paper: “ The appearance of this work motivated the present – shall I say lecture or general confession?

The orthodox solution to the measurement problem (i.e., Schrödinger ’ s cat paradox) is to add to the laws of QM the postulate that whenever a measurement occurs, Schrödinger ’ s equation is no longer valid, and the wavefunction “ jumps ” or “ collapses ” from a superposition (cat alive and dead) into a state corresponding to a de ﬁ nite measurement outcome (cat alive or dead).
In particular, one can recognize a certain tradition (starting perhaps with Schrödinger ’ s cat) to invoke animals to ridicule the vagueness and anthropocentrism of the orthodox collapse postulate.
” Bohr (1935) reacts to EPR with an essay that has since become infamous for its obscurity but is noteworthy for its title.
